questions.question: Observe the feasibility of the application of patrimonial state model in pre-modern Chinese society. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Observe the feasibility of the application of patrimonial state model in pre -modern Chinese society.
  • [An] / [CO2] – Patrimonialism is a form of political organization where authority is based on the direct
  • or indirect personal power exercised by the ruler – Rule alone or as part of an oligarchy – Personal control
  • over the administrative staffs – Support of intellectual and moral elements like priests or philosophers
  • and military – recognition of ruler as the chief landlord or owner of all land – unchallenged legal authority
  • – These features could identify in premodern Chinese polity where Emperor was all powerful, administer
  • with a Grand Secretariat and Bords – moralist and idealist Confucius teachings regarded society as a loose
  • aggregate of family units with ruling family at the head – Traditional customs were employed to establish
  • control over state – Peripheral regions and neighbouring territories were brought under con trol by
  • employing the idea of Chinese emperor as elder brother of the rulers there.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Why a static society without private property has been employed on Asian societies in the Asiatic Mode of Production. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Why a static society without private property has been employed on Asian societies in
  • the Asiatic Mode of Production. [An] / [CO2] - The concept of the Asiatic Mode of
  • Production (AMP) was developed by Karl Marx to explain the socio-economic structure of
  • many ancient Asian societies-private ownership of land was either absent or very limited,
  • while land was owned by the state or by village communities.The village community
  • functioned as a self-sufficient economic unit,-Agriculture depended heavily on large-scale
  • irrigation works, canals and reservoirs, which required central coordination.The
  • organisation and maintenance of irrigation systems were controlled by a powerful
  • centralised state, often referred to as Oriental Despotism.The ruling authority appropriated
  • surplus mainly through taxation and tribute, rather than through feudal rent.Since village
  • communities remained largely unchanged for centuries, and social structures showed little
  • internal dynamism.The absence of private landed property prevented the emergence of
  • feudal landlordism similar to that of medieval Europe.
questions.source_exam: III Semester MGU-UGP-(Hons) 2024 Admission Regular(Special Examination) Examination July 2026

questions.question: List out the qualitative changes occurred in the field of biological science during scientific revolution. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• List out the qualitative changes occurred in the field of biological science during the
  • Scientific Revolution. [U] / [CO4] - The Scientific Revolution replaced medieval beliefs
  • based on Aristotle and Galen with knowledge derived from observation, experimentation
  • and reason.Andreas Vesalius published De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543), correcting
  • many errors in human anatomy through direct dissection.William Harvey published De
  • Motu Cordis (1628), proving that blood circulates continuously through the body and that
  • the heart functions as a pump.The invention and improvement of the compound
  • microscope opened entirely new areas of biological investigation.Robert Hooke published
  • Micrographia (1665), in which he described microscopic structures and introduced the
  • term "cell" after observing cork tissue.Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using powerful
  • microscopes of his own design, observed bacteria, protozoa, sperm cells and red blood
  • cells, earning recognition as the Father of Microbiology.Scientific classification of plants
  • and animals became increasingly systematic through detailed observation and
  • comparison.Biology gradually emerged as an independent scientific discipline based on
  • experimentation rather than traditional authority.

questions.question: Analyse the outlook of the European Enlightenment towards the religious institutions. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the outlook of the European Enlightenment towards the religious institutions.
  • [An] / [CO3] -.Enlightenment thinkers challenged the political and religious authority
  • exercised by the Roman Catholic Church.They criticised superstition, dogmatism, clerical
  • privilege and the suppression of free enquiry-Voltaire attacked religious intolerance,
  • fanaticism and corruption within the Church, advocating freedom of belief and
  • expression.John Locke, in his Letter Concerning Toleration (1689), argued that the state
  • should not interfere with individual religious beliefs.Many Enlightenment thinkers supported
  • Deism, believing that God created the universe but did not intervene continuously in
  • human affairs.Denis Diderot, through the publication of the Encyclopédie, spread scientific
  • knowledge and criticised ecclesiastical authority.Enlightenment philosophers advocated
  • the separation of Church and State, limiting the influence of religion in political affairs.

questions.question: Discuss the role of English Civil Wars in the development of the parliamentary democracy. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the role of English Civil Wars in the development of parliamentary democracy.
  • [U] / [CO4] - Charles I followed the Divine Right TheoryThe supporters of the King were
  • known as Royalists (Cavaliers), while the supporters of Parliament were called
  • Parliamentarians (Roundheads).Oliver Cromwell organised the New Model Army (1645),
  • which became the strongest military force of Parliament.The Battle of Naseby (1645)
  • decisively defeated the Royalist army and ensured Parliamentary supremacy in the
  • war.Charles I was executed in 1649, ending the idea of the absolute authority of the
  • monarchy.England was declared a Commonwealth (1649–1653) under parliamentary rule
  • after the abolition of the monarchy and the House of Lords.Oliver Cromwell assumed the
  • office of Lord Protector (1653–1658) under the Protectorate.The Restoration (1660)
  • brought Charles II back to the throne, but Parliament continued to exercise increasing
  • influence over governance.The Glorious Revolution (1688) peacefully replaced James II
  • with William III and Mary II, establishing parliamentary supremacy.The Bill of Rights (1689)
  • prohibited the monarch from suspending laws, levying taxes or maintaining a standing
  • army without the consent of Parliament.The Toleration Act (1689) granted limited religious
  • freedom to Protestant dissenters and reduced religious conflicts in politics.The Act of
  • Settlement (1701) ensured parliamentary control over succession to the English
  • throne.These constitutional developments established the principle of constitutional
  • monarchy, in which the monarch ruled according to law and with the consent of
  • Parliament.The English Civil Wars and the constitutional settlements that followed laid the
  • foundation for the growth of modern parliamentary democracy in Britain.

questions.question: Observe the nature and working of the mercantilist system in Europe / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Observe the nature and working of the mercantilist system in Europe [U] / [CO5] – mercantilism is
  • an economic nationalism – A system of political economy that sought to enrich the country by restraining
  • imports and encouraging exports to achieve a “favourable” balance of trade that would bring gold and
  • silver into the country and also to maintain domestic employment - Most of the mercantilist policies were
  • the outgrowth of the relationship between the governments of the nation-states and their mercantile classes
  • - government assisted local industry by imposing tariffs, quotas, and prohibitions on imports of goods that
  • competed with local manufacturers – prohibited the export of tools and equi pment and emigration of
  • labour – bounty given to ship builders and merchants - In France, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, the minister of
  • finance under Louis XIV from 1661 to 1683, increased port duties on foreign vessels entering French
  • ports and provided bounties to French shipbuilders - In England, the Navigation Act of 1651 prohibited
  • foreign vessels from engaging in coastal trade in England and required that all goods imported from the
  • continent of Europe be carried on either an English vessel or a vessel registered in the country of or igin
  • of the goods - The Staple Act of 1663 extended the Navigation Act by requiring that all colonial exports
  • to Europe be landed through an English port before being re-exported to Europe. Navigation policies by
  • France, England, and other powers were directed primarily again st the Dutch, who dominated
  • commercial marine activity in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

questions.question: Analyse the theoretical framework of Immanuel Wallerstein in explaining the working of capitalist system. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the theoretical framework of Immanuel Wallerstein in explaining the working of
  • capitalist system. [E] / [CO5] - Immanuel Wallerstein developed the World-Systems Theory
  • in the 1970s.He explained capitalism as a world economic system rather than a collection
  • of separate national economies.The modern world-system emerged during the sixteenth
  • century with European expansion.The capitalist world economy is organised through an
  • international division of labour.Wallerstein classified countries into Core, Semi-Periphery
  • and Periphery.Core countries possess advanced industries, technology and financial
  • resources.Periphery countries mainly supply raw materials, agricultural products and
  • cheap labour.Semi-periphery countries occupy an intermediate position between the Core
  • and Periphery.Core countries exploit the resources and labour of peripheral regions
  • through unequal exchange.Colonialism and imperialism strengthened the expansion of the
  • capitalist world economy.Capital accumulation remains concentrated in the Core.The
  • world-system is dynamic, and countries may shift between categories over
  • time.Wallerstein rejected the idea that societies develop independently.His theory
  • emphasises global economic interdependence and unequal development.

questions.question: Examine the feasibility of the application of the patrimonial model in analysing pre-modern Asian societies. / [CO2] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the feasibility of the application of the patrimonial model in analysing pre-
  • modern Asian societies. [An] / [CO2] -The Patrimonial Model was developed by Max
  • Weber to explain traditional systems of authority.Patrimonial rule is based on personal
  • authority, loyalty and hereditary power.Administrative officials function as personal
  • servants of the ruler rather than as independent bureaucrats.Political authority is closely
  • linked with ownership of land and control over resources.The ruler exercises authority
  • through personal relationships rather than impersonal legal institutions.Many historians
  • have applied the patrimonial model to explain pre-modern Asian kingdoms.It has been
  • used to study states such as Mughal India, Imperial China and the Ottoman Empire.The
  • model explains the concentration of political authority in the ruler and the dependence of
  • officials on royal patronage.It also highlights the importance of kinship, loyalty and
  • personal service in governance.However, critics argue that Asian societies were diverse
  • and cannot be explained by a single model.Many Asian states possessed sophisticated
  • administrative institutions and regional variations.Economic, social and cultural differences
  • limit the universal application of the patrimonial model.
